sentences.text: This large plant-eating dinosaur grew to a length exceeding 9 meters and a mass surpassing 5 metric tons.
Its most defining feature is a prominent cranial crest located at the back of the head, formed by the premaxilla and nasal bones.
Among the three recognized species, P. tubicen stands out as the largest.
The holotype of P. walkeri measures approximately 9.45 meters in length.
The most prominent theory suggests the crest acted as a natural resonator for sound production.
Evidence indicates this animal experienced a very rapid growth rate, reaching maturity in about one year.
William Parks first described the genus Parasaurolophus in 1922.
The type specimen, cataloged as ROM 768, was discovered in 1920 near Sand Creek along the Red Deer River in Alberta.
A juvenile individual, nicknamed Joe and numbered RAM 14000, was formally described in 2013.
The animal could walk on two or four legs, likely preferring to forage quadrupedally but running bipedally.
As a large herbivore, it possessed a skull capable of a grinding motion similar to chewing.
Dental batteries contained hundreds of teeth that were continuously replaced, with only a few in use at any given time.
Hundreds of teeth were arranged in columns and replaced as they wore down.
This wear resulted from a sophisticated masticatory apparatus that allowed it to grind food before swallowing.
The crest is believed to have served multiple purposes, including sexual attraction, communication during danger, and thermoregulation.
The long, side-flattened tail suggests the animal could swim.
One specimen of P. walkeri displays a V-shaped gap or notch in the vertebrae at the base of the neck, which might be a pathology.
The skeleton of P. walkeri also shows a V-shaped notch or gap in the vertebrae at the base of the neck.
Research suggests juveniles likely had small, rounded crests that grew rapidly as they approached sexual maturity.
The type species P. walkeri was named by William Parks in honor of Sir Byron Edmund Walker.
It is classified as a member of the lambeosaurine subfamily within the hadrosaurids, distinct from the hadrosaurine Saurolophus.
Parasaurolophus was quickly assigned to the hadrosaurid subfamily Lambeosaurinae, whereas Saurolophus is considered a Hadrosaurinae.
The genus belongs to the parent group Parasaurolophini.
Parasaurolophus lived in western North America and possibly Asia during the Late Cretaceous period, approximately 76.5 to 73 million years ago.
In the Dinosaur Park Formation, its habitat was a low-relief area of rivers and floodplains that became swampy and influenced by marine conditions.
When the species existed, the Fruitland Formation was a swampy lowland area close to the shore of the Cretaceous Interior Seaway.
The plateau where it lived was an ancient floodplain with large channels, wetland swamps, ponds, and lakes, bordered by highlands.
The animal may have inhabited upland areas where it nested or fed.
It has been debated whether P. cyrtocristatus represents a female of P. walkeri or P. tubicen, though some studies argue against this due to differences in age and anatomy.
Many hypotheses regarding the function of the Parasaurolophus cranial crest have been proposed, though most have been discredited.
James Hopson suggested that P. cyrtocristatus represented the female form of P. tubicen due to its smaller crest.
Early researchers proposed that the crest of Parasaurolophus was an adaptation for an aquatic lifestyle, a hypothesis common until the 1960s.
